The early life history of Striped herring (Lile stolifera) begins with the reproductive output of adults. Under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 25.6 °C [T = 25.6 °C], gravid females were observed to release between 180 and 182 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = between 180 and 182 eggs per spawning event], with spawning occurring approximately once per day [F_R_i = spawning occurring approximately once per day]. The maximum daily reproduction rate is approximately 181 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 181 eggs per day]. The fertilised ova are small and pelagic, and upon eclosion, the prolarvae emerge at a remarkably diminutive size. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae have a wet weight at birth of just 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams], a mass that underscores the extreme altriciality of the larval stage. This initial mass necessitates a rapid yolk absorption phase; the depletion of endogenous yolk is typically complete within three to four days post-hatching, at which point the larva must successfully capture its first prey to avoid starvation. The point of no return is generally reached by day eight under these thermal conditions, highlighting the critical window for the onset of exogenous feeding.

As the larvae progress through the pelagic larval phase, their growth trajectory becomes tightly coupled to prey availability and water temperature. During the preflexion and flexion stages, body length increases steadily, and morphological differentiation proceeds rapidly. The total length at puberty for Striped herring has been estimated from field-collected specimens at 10.6 centimeters [Lp = 10.6 centimeters], a size threshold that marks the onset of gonadal recrudescence. This length is attained after a period of several months of sustained somatic growth, during which the larvae metamorphose and transition into the juvenile stage. At 25.6 °C [T = 25.6 °C], the juvenile period is comparatively brief, with individuals reaching reproductive maturity within their first year. The relatively small size at puberty, which is approximately two-thirds of the maximum adult length, suggests an early investment in reproduction, a common strategy among small, short-lived clupeiforms subject to high natural mortality.

The maximum recorded body size for this species, based on extensive survey data from the Gulf of California, is 15.9 centimeters [Li = 15.9 centimeters] in total length. Individuals approaching this ultimate total length are rare and typically represent the oldest age classes within a population. In conjunction with this linear dimension, the ultimate wet weight of the species reaches approximately 50 grams [Wwi = approximately 50 grams] in large, well-conditioned adults. This allometric relationship suggests a relatively fusiform body shape, optimised for sustained swimming in pelagic environments. The correspondence between length and weight is well described by a power-law relationship, and the maximum mass is seldom exceeded, likely constrained by the energetic demands of foraging in a seasonally variable environment. Field observations indicate that very few individuals surpass the 15-centimeter mark, suggesting that size-selective predation or senescence imposes a ceiling on attainable body size.

Reproductive investment in Striped herring is further clarified by examining body mass at the onset of maturity. At the point where females begin vitellogenesis and males initiate spermiation, the average wet weight at puberty is 14.4 grams [Wwp = 14.4 grams]. This represents a substantial multiple of the 0.00018-gram birth mass (0.00018 grams) [Wwb = 0.00018 grams], reflecting the enormous somatic growth required before reproductive function is activated. The allocation of resources toward gonadal development at this size is a critical life-history decision; females putting energy into egg production must balance this against the need for continued somatic growth to reach the ultimate wet weight of approximately 50 grams [Wwi = approximately 50 grams]. In the warm waters of its native habitat, typically at 25.6 °C [T = 25.6 °C], this trade-off is mediated by a high metabolic rate, which in turn drives a rapid turnover of energy reserves and supports a relatively high fecundity for a fish of this moderate size.

Longevity data for Striped herring, derived from otolith-based age estimation, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years] for individuals maintained under optimal conditions at 25.6 °C [T = 25.6 °C]. This lifespan of 1825 days [am = 1825 days] is typical for a small-bodied, short-lived clupeiform species occupying a low trophic level in tropical and subtropical marine ecosystems at a temperature of 25.6 °C [T = 25.6 °C]. The combination of early maturation at 10.6 centimeters [Lp = 10.6 centimeters] total length, rapid growth to an ultimate total length of 15.9 centimeters [Li = 15.9 centimeters], and an annual reproductive output that can total hundreds of eggs per female underscores a life-history strategy geared toward high turnover. The species faces substantial predation pressure throughout its life, from larval stages through to the adult phase, and the relatively brief maximum lifespan of approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years] likely reflects an evolutionary response to this high extrinsic mortality, favouring early and prolific reproduction over somatic persistence at a temperature of 25.6 °C [T = 25.6 °C].
